claim: HBV infection is a major global health problem.
source: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major global health problem.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about HBV's public health impact.

claim: Currently-available therapies are ineffective in curing chronic HBV infection.
source: Currently-available therapies are ineffective in curing chronic HBV infection.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the limitations of current HBV therapies.

claim: HBV and HDV infect hepatocytes via binding of the preS1 domain of its large envelope protein to NTCP.
source: HBV and its satellite hepatitis D virus (HDV) infect hepatocytes via binding of the preS1 domain of its large envelope protein to sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Yan et al., 2012; Li, 2015) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Novel human monoclonal antibodies were developed that block the engagement of preS1 with NTCP.
source: Here, we developed novel human monoclonal antibodies that block the engagement of preS1 with NTCP and neutralize HBV and HDV with high potency.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The antibody 2H5-A14 functions at picomolar level.
source: One antibody, 2H5-A14, functions at picomolar level and exhibited neutralization-activity-mediated prophylactic effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 2 and related text.

claim: 2H5-A14 exhibited neutralization-activity-mediated prophylactic effects.
source: One antibody, 2H5-A14, functions at picomolar level and exhibited neutralization-activity-mediated prophylactic effects.
evidence: This is supported by data from mouse prophylaxis experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: 2H5-A14 acts therapeutically by eliciting antibody-Fc-dependent immunological effector functions.
source: It also acts therapeutically by eliciting antibody-Fc-dependent immunological effector functions that impose durable suppression of viral infection in HBV-infected mice, resulting in reductions in the levels of the small envelope antigen and viral DNA, with no emergence of escape mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing 2H5-A14 with its Fc-mutant variant (2H5-A14-DANA) in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: 2H5-A14 treatment results in reductions in the levels of the small envelope antigen and viral DNA in HBV-infected mice.
source: It also acts therapeutically by eliciting antibody-Fc-dependent immunological effector functions that impose durable suppression of viral infection in HBV-infected mice, resulting in reductions in the levels of the small envelope antigen and viral DNA, with no emergence of escape mutants.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 5 measuring HBsAg and HBV DNA levels.

claim: No escape mutants emerged during 2H5-A14 treatment.
source: It also acts therapeutically by eliciting antibody-Fc-dependent immunological effector functions that impose durable suppression of viral infection in HBV-infected mice, resulting in reductions in the levels of the small envelope antigen and viral DNA, with no emergence of escape mutants.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data of the HBV L gene from treated mice described in the Results section and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Human HBV infects more people than HCV and HIV combined.
source: Human hepatitis B virus (HBV) infects more people than does Hepatitis C virus (HCV) and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) combined (World Health Organization, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2016.

claim: 240 million people are chronically infected with HBV.
source: Despite the fact that there is an effective prophylactic HBV vaccine, 240 million people are chronically infected.
evidence: This is a factual statement that draws from established epidemiological data.

claim: HBV carriers are at high risk of developing severe liver diseases ranging from chronic hepatic insufficiency to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: HBV carriers are at high risk of developing severe liver diseases ranging from chronic hepatic insufficiency to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (World Health Organization, 2016; Schweitzer et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2016 and Schweitzer et al., 2015.

claim: Current therapies are inadequate for treating chronic HBV infection.
source: Current therapies are inadequate for treating chronic HBV infection.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent discussion of limitations of interferon and NUC therapies.

claim: Interferon alpha therapies have a curative effect in a small portion of patients.
source: For example, the immune-modulatory interferon alpha therapies have a curative effect in a small portion of patients; nucleos(t)ide analog (NUC) therapies can suppress viral replication but hardly achieve sustained virological control after treatment withdrawal and are non-curative (Lok et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lok et al., 2016.

claim: Nucleos(t)ide analog therapies can suppress viral replication but hardly achieve sustained virological control after treatment withdrawal and are non-curative.
source: For example, the immune-modulatory interferon alpha therapies have a curative effect in a small portion of patients; nucleos(t)ide analog (NUC) therapies can suppress viral replication but hardly achieve sustained virological control after treatment withdrawal and are non-curative (Lok et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lok et al., 2016.

claim: Approximately 15 million HBV carriers are co-infected with HDV.
source: Approximately 15 million of HBV carriers are co-infected with HDV, which accelerates disease progression and exacerbates disease severity.
evidence: This is a factual epidemiological statement that draws from established knowledge.

claim: HDV co-infection accelerates disease progression and exacerbates disease severity.
source: Approximately 15 million of HBV carriers are co-infected with HDV, which accelerates disease progression and exacerbates disease severity.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical knowledge about HDV co-infection.

claim: No effective therapies are currently available for HBV patients co-infected with HDV.
source: No effective therapies are currently available for HBV patients co-infected with HDV, and there are no anti-viral therapies that specifically target HDV (Rizzetto, 2015; Hughes et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rizzetto, 2015; Hughes et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2015.

claim: HBV cccDNA serves as both the intermediate for viral replication and as a viral persistence reservoir.
source: Upon entering hepatocytes, HBV covalent closed circular DNA (cccDNA) is generated in the nucleus of infected cells, and this cccDNA serves as both the intermediate for viral replication and as a viral persistence reservoir.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about HBV biology.

claim: Curing chronic hepatitis B would require either elimination or permanently silencing of the cccDNA from hepatocytes and/or elimination of the infected hepatocytes carrying cccDNA.
source: It is believed that curing chronic hepatitis B (CHB) would require either elimination or permanently silencing of the cccDNA from hepatocytes and/or elimination of the infected hepatocytes carrying cccDNA (Zeisel et al., 2015; Seeger and Mason, 2016; Liang et al., 2015; Block et al., 2013; Gane, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zeisel et al., 2015; Seeger and Mason, 2016; Liang et al., 2015; Block et al., 2013; Gane, 2017.

claim: Immunotherapies based on human monoclonal antibodies have achieved remarkable clinical success in treating multiple cancers and various autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.
source: Immunotherapies based on human monoclonal antibodies (mAb) have achieved remarkable clinical success in treating multiple cancers and various autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the clinical success of mAb therapies.

claim: Chronic viral infectious diseases can be treated via mAb-based immunotherapy.
source: More recent efforts have shown that chronic viral infectious diseases can be treated via mAb-based immunotherapy; studies have reported promising clinical outcomes using a mAb with broad and potent activity in neutralizing HIV (Schoofs et al., 2016; Scheid et al., 2016; Caskey et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schoofs et al., 2016; Scheid et al., 2016; Caskey et al., 2015.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies exert a variety of immunological 'effector' functions, including clearance of circulatory viruses and mediating cytotoxic killing or phagocytosis of infected cells.
source: Neutralizing antibodies (nAbs), in addition to their capacity to specifically block viral entry via Fab (fragment of antigen binding) recognition of virus, have been found to exert a variety of immunological 'effector' functions, including clearance of circulatory viruses as well as by mediating cytotoxic killing or phagocytosis of infected cells (DiLillo et al., 2014; Corti et al., 2011; Bournazos et al., 2014; Bruel et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Hessell et al., 2007), or even possibly triggering sustained host immune responses in vivo (Schoofs et al., 2016; Pelegrin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to DiLillo et al., 2014; Corti et al., 2011; Bournazos et al., 2014; Bruel et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Hessell et al., 2007; Schoofs et al., 2016; Pelegrin et al., 2015.

claim: Virus-infected cells can be eliminated by antibody dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) and phagocytosis (ADCP) through interaction of the Fc of an antibody with its cognate Fcγ receptors expressed on immune cells.
source: For example, just as with cancer cells, virus-infected cells can be eliminated by antibody dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) and phagocytosis (ADCP) through interaction of the Fc (fragment crystallizable domain) of an antibody with its cognate Fcγ receptors (FcγRs) expressed on immune cells.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about antibody effector functions.

claim: The preS1 domain of the L protein specifically binds to NTCP in hepatocytes and mediates viral entry of HBV and HDV.
source: We discovered that the preS1 domain of the L protein specifically binds to the liver bile acid transporter sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) in hepatocytes and thusly mediates viral entry of HBV and HDV (Yan et al., 2012; Li, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yan et al., 2012 and Li, 2015, which are the authors' own prior work.

claim: Six nAbs that were effective in neutralizing HBV were identified from a large non-immune phage display antibody library.
source: By employing HepG2-hNTCP cell-based in vitro HBV infection systems (Sun et al., 2016), we identified six nAbs that were effective in neutralizaling HBV, but each differed in its potency (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The six identified nAbs recognized four unique epitopes.
source: Epitope mapping by direct binding and competition ELISA assays showed that these nAbs recognized four unique epitopes, represented by #71, 2H5, m1Q and #15, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2A–C.

claim: The neutralization potency of the nAbs correlated with the location of their epitopes in relation to the receptor binding site in preS1.
source: The neutralization potency of these nAbs correlated with the location of their epitopes in relation to the receptor binding site (RBS) in preS1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the epitope mapping and neutralization data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: 2H5 and m1Q neutralized HDV infection in HepG2-hNTCP cells.
source: 2H5 and m1Q were also able to neutralize HDV infection in HepG2-hNTCP cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 2H5 was slightly more potent in neutralizing HBV and HDV than m1Q.
source: As 2H5 was slightly more potent in neutralizing HBV and HDV than m1Q, we selected 2H5 for further characterization and optimization.
evidence: This is based on comparison of neutralization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The crystal structure of the scFv of 2H5 in complex with the preS1 peptide was solved at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: The complex structure was determined by molecular replacement and refined at 2.5 Å resolution to an R-factor of 0.23 and an R-free value of 0.28 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1C-E.

claim: In the complex structure, residues 20–27 of the preS1 peptide adopt a U-shaped conformation and are situated in a pocket formed by five CDR loops from both VH and VL of 2H5.
source: The 8-residue peptide adopts a U-shaped conformation and is situated in a pocket formed by five complementarity-determining-region (CDR) loops from both the variable heavy (VH) and light chains (VL) of 2H5 (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: The interface between 2H5 scFv and the preS1 peptide buries a solvent accessible area of about 460.8 Å2.
source: The interface between 2H5 scFv and the preS1 peptide buries a solvent accessible area of about 460.8 Å2, accounting for 54.6% of the total peptide surface area.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement derived from the crystal structure analysis.

claim: Asp20, Pro21, and Phe23 are key binding residues in the 2H5 epitope.
source: However, three 16-mer variants of the preS1 peptide that had a key residue (Asp20, Pro21, or Phe23) mutated to alanine failed to compete the full-length preS1 peptide for binding to 2H5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The 2H5 epitope is highly conserved among HBV genotypes.
source: Of note, sequence alignment showed that 2H5 epitope is highly conserved among HBV genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that 2H5 can potentially provide broad protection against the vast majority of HBV genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: G24R mutation of the preS1 peptide had no effect on binding to 2H5.
source: Although residue 24 in the 2H5 epitope is variable among different HBV genotypes (e.g., Gly24 in genotypes A and C; Lys24 or Arg24 in all other genotypes, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), G24R mutation of the preS1 peptide had no effect on binding to 2H5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), consistent with our observation from the complex structure that Gly24 does not make direct contact with 2H5.
evidence: This claim is supported by binding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and structural analysis.

claim: Prophylactic administration of 2H5 IgG1 resulted in more than one log reduction of HDV viral titer in mouse livers compared to untreated controls.
source: Using this model, prophylactic administration of 2H5 IgG1 (1 hr before HDV viral challenge) resulted in a more than one log reduction of the viral titer in mouse livers as compared to untreated controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F from the hNTCP-Tg mouse model.

claim: 2H5 treatment at 20 mg/kg was not able to completely block HDV infection in mouse livers.
source: Nevertheless, 2H5 treatment was not able to completely block HDV infection in mouse livers, even at a 20 mg/kg dose.
evidence: This is based on the HDV infection data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: VH chain shuffling led to the identification of 16 Abs with higher binding affinity than 2H5.
source: VH chain shuffling by fixing the variable light (VL) chain of 2H5 and pairing it with a repertoire of naturally-occurring variable heavy (VH) genes (~1×1010) led to the identification of 16 Abs with higher binding affinity.
evidence: This is supported by the antibody engineering data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four top nAbs (2H5-31, 2H5-32, 2H5-A14, and 2H5-A21) had about 100-fold improvement in binding activity relative to 2H5.
source: ELISA assays revealed that the four top (2H5-31, 2H5-32, 2H5-A14, and 2H5-A21) nAbs had about 100-fold improvement in binding activity relative to 2H5 (Figure 2-figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The four top nAbs had about 20-fold increases in neutralizing activity against HBV and about 100-fold increases against HDV relative to 2H5.
source: Further neutralization assays revealed that, relative to 2H5, these four nAbs all had about 20-fold increases in neutralizing activity against HBV and about 100-fold increases against HDV, and their HBV neutralization IC50 values were all lower than 50 pM under the conditions tested (Figure 2-figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C.

claim: 2H5-A14 targets the same epitope as 2H5.
source: Competition ELISA assays showed that 2H5-A14 had almost the same peptide competition pattern as did 2H5, and mutation of G24R of preS1 did not affect 2H5-A14 binding activity, indicating that 2H5-A14 targets the same epitope as does 2H5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by competition ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: 2H5-A14 inhibited the binding of FITC-labeled preS1 to HepG2-hNTCP cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: An immunofluorescence staining assay showed that 2H5-A14 inhibited the binding of FITC-labeled preS1 to HepG2-hNTCP cells in a dose-dependent manner, whereas an isotype-matched control Ab did not (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The neutralization mechanism of 2H5-A14 likely involves blocking of viral entry by interfering with the binding of NTCP and preS1.
source: This result indicates that the neutralization mechanism of 2H5-A14 likely involves blocking of viral entry by interfering with the binding of NTCP and preS1, probably owing to steric hindrance at or near the preS1 receptor binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competition data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 2H5-A14 potently neutralized HBV genotypes B, C, and D.
source: HBV has 10 known genotypes, all of which differ from each other by at least 8% at DNA sequence level (Sunbul, 2014). Genotypes B, C, and D represent the major epidemic genotypes, and 2H5-A14 potently neutralized all three of these genotypes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 2H5-A14 had more than 1000-fold stronger neutralization activity than HBIG against HBV infection.
source: Assays using a HepG2-hNTCP cell-based HBV infection system showed that 2H5-A14 had more than 1000-fold stronger neutralization activity than did HBIG against infection with recombinant HBV (Figure 2C) and HDV (Figure 2D), as well as against infection with six HBV primary isolates derived from HBV-infected patients (genotype C) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutralization comparison data shown in Figure 2C, 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: 2H5-A14 had about 200-fold stronger neutralizing activity against HBV than KR127.
source: 2H5-A14 also had about 200-fold stronger neutralizing activity against HBV than did KR127, and 50-fold stronger anti-HBV activity than did either m47-D or m47 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutralization comparison data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 2H5-A14 showed similar neutralization potency against a clinical viral isolate from an HBV-infected patient (genotype B) in primary human hepatocytes.
source: Consistently, in a primary human hepatocyte (PHHs) infection system, 2H5-A14 showed similar neutralization potency against a clinical viral isolate from an HBV-infected patient (genotype B) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutralization data in PHHs shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The epitope of 2H5-A14 is highly conserved and can neutralize the vast majority (>95%) of HBV virus strains.
source: Given this, it is reasonable to extrapolate that 2H5-A14 can likely neutralize the vast majority (>95%) of HBV virus strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis and neutralization data across multiple genotypes.

claim: A 15 mg/kg dose of 2H5-A14 completely blocked HDV infection in NTCP gene-edited mice.
source: A 15 mg/kg dose of 2H5-A14 completely blocked HDV infection, reducing HDV titers in liver to below their limit of detection at day six after HDV challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the NTCP gene-edited mouse model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 3 mg/kg and 0.6 mg/kg doses of 2H5-A14 reduced HDV titers by 99.4% and 98.5%, respectively, in NTCP gene-edited mice.
source: Notably, 3 mg/kg and 0.6 mg/kg doses reduced HDV titers by 99.4% and 98.5%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the NTCP gene-edited mouse model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A high dose of HBIG (100 IU/kg) only reduced HDV titers by 90% in NTCP gene-edited mice.
source: In contrast, even a high dose of HBIG (100 IU/kg) only reduced HDV titers by 90%, which was still insufficient to prevent HDV infection (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the NTCP gene-edited mouse model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A single administration of 2H5-A14 (15 mg/kg) one day prior to HBV challenge completely protected hFRG mice from HBV infection.
source: A single administration of 2H5-A14 (15 mg/kg) one day prior to HBV challenge completely protected mice from HBV infection, as indicated by the levels of all of the virological markers in serum samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the hFRG mouse model shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Biweekly 2H5-A14 treatment (20 mg/kg) greatly reduced all virological markers in sera of HBV-infected hFRG mice compared to infection-only control and HBIG treatment groups.
source: Therapeutically, biweekly 2H5-A14 treatment (20 mg/kg) greatly reduced all of the virological markers in sera as compared to infection-only control and to the HBIG treatment groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the hFRG mouse model shown in Figure 3C.

claim: By the end of the experiment (37 dpi), 2H5-A14 treatment resulted in three log reductions in the HBV DNA and RNA levels relative to the two control groups in hFRG mice.
source: Remarkably, by the end of the experiment (37 dpi), 2H5-A14 treatment resulted in three log reductions in the HBV DNA and RNA levels relative to the two control groups (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the hFRG mouse model shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Liver tissues from 2H5-A14 prophylaxis group animals had no detectable HBsAg, HBcAg, HBV DNA, cccDNA, or RNA.
source: Consistent with our sera-based measurements, liver tissues from 2H5-A14 prophylaxis group animals had no detectable HBsAg and HBcAg or HBV DNA, cccDNA, or RNA; while both the infection vehicle control and HBIG treatment groups had strong signals for these markers; liver tissues from 2H5-A14 treatment had greatly reduced HBsAg and HBcAg, and had almost undetectable levels of HBV DNA and RNA (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC, Southern blot, and Northern blot data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: 2H5-A14 induced ADCC via NK cells expressing FcγRIIIa.
source: 2H5-A14 but not an isotype-matched control antibody treatment resulted in a dose-dependent cytotoxic effect against CHO-59C cells; no such effect was observed for the CHO-59C-mut control cells, demonstrating that NK cell-mediated ADCC requires the presence of the 2H5-A14 epitope on target cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADCC assay data using NK92-MIhCD16 cells shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 2H5-A14 induced ADCC against HBV-infected HepG2-hNTCP cells via NK cells.
source: Using the same ADCC assay, we also demonstrated that 2H5-A14, but not the 2H5-A14-DANA variant, caused ADCC against HBV-infected cells. The HepG2-hNTCP cells infected by HBV were specifically killed by NK cells, whereas the HepG2-hNTCP cells uninfected by HBV were spared from NK cell killing (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADCC assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 2H5-A14 mediated both ADCC and ADCP via human macrophages.
source: When fully differentiated human macrophages were mixed with target cells (293F-59C, see materials and methods) expressing the 2H5-A14 epitope on their surface, both ADCP and ADCC were observed following treatment with wild type 2H5-A14 but not with the 2H5-A14-DANA variant (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADCC and ADCP assay data using human macrophages shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 2H5-A14 mediated ADCP via mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: Similar results were obtained using mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) as effector cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADCP assay data using mouse BMDMs shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: 2H5-A14 did not induce CDC against target cells.
source: In the presence of complement sera (from rabbit or human), 2H5-A14 did not cause cell lysis of CHO-59C cells. Under the same testing conditions, anti-CD20 (Rituximab) and an anti-GPC3 chimeric antibody (GC33) that are known to cause CDC all induced target-specific CDC (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A) as previously reported (Nakano et al., 2009; van Meerten et al., 2006). Thus, 2H5-A14 is not competent to induce CDC against target cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by CDC assay data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: 2H5-A14 has very weak binding activity to both human and mouse C1q.
source: Consistently, 2H5-A14 has very weak binding activity to both human- and mouse C1q (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by C1q binding assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: 2H5-A14-DANA and 2H5-A14 showed similar prophylactic efficacy in NTCP gene-edited mice, both offering complete protection from HDV infection at a 5 mg/kg dose.
source: In the Ntcp gene-edited homozygous FVB mice, 2H5-A14-DANA and 2H5-A14 showed similar prophylactic efficacy: both offered complete protection from HDV infection at a 5 mg/kg dose (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the NTCP gene-edited mouse model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Fab-mediated neutralization, rather than Fc-mediated effector function, is primarily responsible for preventing viral infection in the prophylaxis setting.
source: This result suggests that Fab-mediated neutralization, rather than the Fc-mediated effector function, is primarily responsible for preventing viral infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of 2H5-A14 and 2H5-A14-DANA in the prophylaxis model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the 2H5-A14 treatment group, the average HBV DNA titer was ~1.0×10^7/mL and the HBsAg level was ~70 IU/mL at 89 dpi in hFRG mice.
source: In contrast, compared to the control group, the 2H5-A14 treatment group had an about 200-fold reduction in DNA titer (~1.0×107/mL) and a ~ 40000 fold reduction in the HBsAg level (~70 IU/mL) at 89 dpi.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the hFRG mouse treatment study shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment with 2H5-A14 resulted in reductions in both HBV DNA titer and HBsAg levels over time in hFRG mice.
source: Importantly, in contrast to control PBS or 2H5-A14-DANA, treatment with 2H5-A14 resulted in reductions in both HBV DNA titer and HBsAg levels over time, starting from the beginning of the treatment and continuing through the treatment window and 3 weeks after treatment withdrawal, with only a slight rebound at the end of the experiment (4 weeks after treatment withdrawal) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal data from the hFRG mouse treatment study shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 2H5-A14 treatment not only efficiently suppressed the spread of HBV in mice, but could also gradually reduce the extent of an established HBV infection over time.
source: These results showed that 2H5-A14 treatment not only efficiently suppressed the spread of HBV in mice, but could also gradually reduce the extent of an established HBV infection over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the longitudinal data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 2H5-A14-DANA was able to suppress the spread of HBV but did not reduce the extent of an established HBV infection in hFRG mice.
source: In contrast, 2H5-A14-DANA was able to suppress the spread of HBV as compared to the control group, but it did not reduce the extent of an established HBV infection: the levels of HBV DNA and HBsAg at all tested time points after the treatment were all higher than those at the starting point of treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the hFRG mouse treatment study shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Liver tissues from 2H5-A14-treated mice had greatly reduced levels of HBsAg compared to control mice.
source: Consistent with our sera-based measurements, liver tissues from 2H5-A14-treated but not 2H5-A14-DANA-treated mice had greatly reduced levels of HBsAg (IHC assay) comparing to the control mice (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HBV total DNA and cccDNA were undetectable for the 2H5-A14-treatment group by Southern blotting.
source: Southern blotting showed that the HBV total DNA and cccDNA were undetectable for the 2H5-A14-treatment group, whereas strong total DNA and cccDNA signals were observed for the 2H5-A14-DANA and control groups (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: 2H5-A14-treated mice had much lower cccDNA copy numbers than the other two groups by qPCR.
source: Quantification of the cccDNA level in the liver tissues by qPCR further independently confirmed that 2H5-A14-treated mice indeed had much lower cccDNA copy numbers than the other two groups (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The comparison of 2H5-A14 and 2H5-A14-DANA treatments proves that the anti-viral effect of 2H5-A14 results only in part from Fab-mediated neutralization, while Fc-dependent effector functions are critical in conferring its overall therapeutic effect.
source: Moreover, the comparison of the effects of 2H5-A14 and 2H5-A14-DANA treatments side by side clearly proves that the anti-viral effect of 2H5-A14 results only in part from Fab-mediated neutralization, while the Fc-dependent effector functions of 2H5-A14 are particularly critical in conferring its overall therapeutic effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative data of 2H5-A14 and 2H5-A14-DANA shown in Figure 5.

claim: No mutations were found within the antibody's epitope in HBV L genes sequenced from mouse liver tissues after 2H5-A14 treatment.
source: Few random mutations were observed within the L genes in both mouse studies, and it appeared that more mutations were in the 2H5-A14 treatment group than that in the control group, but no mutation was specifically associated with 2H5-A14 treatment and no mutations were found within the antibody's epitope (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The epitope of 2H5-A14 is likely unsusceptible to escape mutation.
source: Although we cannot completely rule out the possibility that 2H5-A14 treatment may induce escape mutants, these results indicate that the epitope of 2H5-A14, a receptor-binding proximal and highly conservative region centered by Phe23, is likely unsusceptible to escape mutation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data and the structural/functional importance of the epitope.

claim: Neither the HBV vaccine nor HBIG are effective in treating persistent HBV infection.
source: In HBV, nAbs against the HBV small (S) envelop protein (HBsAg) constitute the major protective components of both the widely-used recombinant HBV vaccine and of the post-exposure prophylactic blood-derived HBIG. However, neither the vaccine nor HBIG are effective in treating persistent HBV infection (Tsuge et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsuge et al., 2016.

claim: A combination of two monoclonal nAbs against HBsAg (HepeX-B) only exhibited short-term anti-viral effects in animal models and an early phase I human study.
source: A previous study reported that a combination of two monoclonal nAbs against HBsAg (HepeX-B) only exhibited short-term anti-viral effects in animal models and an early phase I human study (Eren et al., 2000; Neumann et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Eren et al., 2000 and Neumann et al., 2010.

claim: A humanized anti-HBsAg nAb was shown to have longer anti-viral effects in mouse models mainly through clearance of Ab-HBsAg immune complexes by phagocytosis.
source: A humanized anti-HBsAg nAb was recently shown to have longer anti-viral effects in mouse models mainly through clearance of the Ab-HBsAg immune complexes by phagocytosis (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: High levels of circulating HBsAg-containing non-infectious subviral particles are commonly present in the blood of chronically-infected HBV patients.
source: High levels of circulating HBsAg-containing non-infectious subviral particles are commonly present in the blood of chronically-infected HBV patients (Seeger et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Seeger et al., 2007.

claim: The L protein is much less abundant in circulation than HBsAg and preferentially present on infectious HBV particles.
source: Compared to the HBsAg, the L protein is much less abundant in circulation and preferentially present on infectious HBV particles (Seeger et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Seeger et al., 2007.

claim: Two anti-preS1 nAbs, BX-182 and KR127, have been shown to prevent HBV infection when injected in chimpanzees prior to HBV challenge.
source: To date, two anti-preS1 nAbs, the murine BX-182 nAb and humanized KR127 nAb, have been shown to be able to prevent HBV infection when injected in chimpanzees prior to HBV challenge (Chi et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chi et al., 2007 and Zhang et al., 2006.

claim: BX-182 is an HBV subtype-specific nAb owing to sequence variations in its epitope (residues 6–10 of preS1, SVPNP).
source: BX-182 is an HBV subtype-specific nAb owing to sequence variations in its epitope (residues 6–10 of preS1, SVPNP).
evidence: This statement reflects knowledge about the specificity of BX-182.

claim: KR127 recognizes residues 37–45 (NSNNPDWDF) of preS1 and has broader neutralizing activity than BX-182, but its potency is limited.
source: KR127 recognizes residues 37–45 (NSNNPDWDF) of preS1 and has broader neutralizing activity than BX-182, but its potency is limited, diminishing its promise for therapy.
evidence: This statement reflects knowledge about KR127's epitope and activity.

claim: 2H5-A14 has potent viral neutralization activity with low picomolar IC50 values in cell cultures.
source: 2H5-A14 has potent viral neutralization activity with low picomolar IC50 values in cell cultures.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 2H5-A14 is extremely effective in protecting mice from de novo HDV and HBV infection.
source: Consistent with this in vitro potency, it is extremely effective in protecting mice from de novo HDV and HBV infection.
evidence: This is supported by prophylaxis data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: 2H5-A14 demonstrated impressive therapeutic efficacy against HBV infection in two independent mouse studies using liver-humanized hFRG mice.
source: Remarkably, 2H5-A14 demonstrated impressive therapeutic efficacy against HBV infection in two independent mouse studies using liver-humanized hFRG mice.
evidence: This is supported by treatment data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Viral neutralization by 2H5-A14 is the dominant mechanism contributing to the protection of mice from HDV infection.
source: Mechanistically, we found that viral neutralization by 2H5-A14 is the dominant mechanism contributing to the protection of mice from HDV infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of 2H5-A14 and 2H5-A14-DANA in the HDV prophylaxis model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Fc-mediated effector functions contribute substantially to the overall antiviral effect of 2H5-A14 against HBV infection in hFRG mice.
source: In contrast, in addition to protecting hepatocytes from viral entry, Fc-mediated effector functions contribute substantially to the overall antiviral effect of 2H5-A14 against HBV infection in hFRG mice.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of 2H5-A14 and 2H5-A14-DANA in the HBV treatment model shown in Figure 5.

claim: The observed effector functions in hFRG model cannot be attributed to NK cells but to FcγR-expressing macrophages or other myeloid cells.
source: hFRG mice lack T and B lymphocytes, and NK cells. NK cells are generally considered to be the main effector cells in mediating ADCC to induce apoptosis in target cells (Wang et al., 2015). The observed effector functions in hFRG model thus cannot be attributed to NK cells but to the remaining immune effector cells in these mice; for example FcγR-expressing macrophages or other meloid cells (e.g. neutraphils) that are capable of killing infected hepatocytes by ADCC and/or ADCP or antibody-dependent scretion of antiviral cytokines or by direct clearance of the antibody-opsonized viruses via phagocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunodeficient nature of hFRG mice and the observed effector functions.

claim: CDC is unlikely involved in the anti-viral effect of 2H5-A14 in HBV-infected hFRG mice.
source: Considering that primary hepatocytes and HBV-infected hepatocytes may be resistant to CDC (Halme et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013), and 2H5-A14 lacked complement C1q binding activity and CDC activity in vitro, CDC is unlikely involved in the anti-viral effect of 2H5-A14 in the HBV-infected hFRG mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on literature citations (Halme et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013) and in vitro CDC data.

claim: Macrophages have been shown to be the major effector cells involved in anti-tumor activity of several mAbs in mice.
source: Macrophages have previosuly been shown to be the major effector cells invovled in anti-tumor activity of several mAbs in mice (Clynes et al., 2000; Hamaguchi et al., 2006; Minard-Colin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Clynes et al., 2000; Hamaguchi et al., 2006; Minard-Colin et al., 2008.

claim: Neutrophils have been reported to be involved in the anti-tumor efficacy of two mAbs in tumor models in mice.
source: Neutrophils have also been reported to be involved in the anti-tumor efficacy of two mAbs in tumor models in mice (Siders et al., 2010; Golay et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Siders et al., 2010 and Golay et al., 2013.

claim: During chronic HBV infection, NK cells have impaired secretion of antiviral cytokines yet are able to maintain their cytotoxicity.
source: During chronic HBV infection, it appears that NK cells have impaired secretion of antiviral cytokines (e.g. IFN-γ) yet are able to maintain their cytotoxicity (Maini and Peppa, 2013; Sun et al., 2015; Shabani et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Maini and Peppa, 2013; Sun et al., 2015; Shabani et al., 2014.

claim: The proportion of FcγR-expressing NK cells in liver (27–75% of total NK cells in liver) is lower than that in blood.
source: The proportion of FcγR-expressing NK cells in liver (27–75% of total NK cells in liver) is lower than that in blood (Burt et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Burt et al., 2009.

claim: Hepatic macrophages include both infiltrating macrophages and liver-resident macrophages (Kupffer cells, accounting for 80–90% of all tissue macrophages in entire body).
source: Hepatic macropahges include both infiltrating macrophages and liver-resident macrophages (Kupffer cells, accounting for 80–90% of all tissue macrophages in entire body [Jenne and Kubes, 2013]).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jenne and Kubes, 2013.

claim: Hepatic macrophages likely retain antibody-dependent effector functions via their expressed FcγRs.
source: Similar to human tumor-associated macrophages, hepatic macropahges likely retain antibody-dependent effector fuctions via their expressed FcγRs (Herter et al., 2014; Grugan et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Herter et al., 2014 and Grugan et al., 2012.

claim: 2H5-A14 treatment resulted in substantial decreases in HBsAg levels in the blood of HBV-infected hFRG mice over time.
source: First, 2H5-A14 treatment resulted in substantial decreases in HBsAg levels in the blood of HBV-infected hFRG mice over time.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Serological HBsAg reduction, and eventually HBsAg loss, is considered as a critical step toward a 'functional cure'.
source: Serological HBsAg reduction, and eventually HBsAg loss, is considered as a critical step toward a 'functional cure'.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about HBV treatment goals.

claim: Current NUCs therapy rarely reduces HBsAg level in CHB patients.
source: Current NUCs therapy rarely reduces HBsAg level in CHB patients.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the limitations of NUC therapy.

claim: The decline of HBsAg by 2H5-A14 cannot be attributed to Ab-mediated clearance of HBsAg from the blood, but to a gradual reduction of established HBV infection.
source: 2H5-A14 specifically targets preS1 but not the vast majority of HBsAg particles, therefore, in contrast to nAbs targeting HBsAg, the decline of HBsAg by 2H5-A14 cannot be attributed to the Ab-mediated clearance of HBsAg from the blood, but to a gradual reduction of established HBV infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of 2H5-A14 and the observed HBsAg reduction.

claim: 2H5-A14 treatment at least effectively suppressed cccDNA accumulation and more likely reduced cccDNA in liver tissues.
source: Second, 2H5-A14 treatment at least effectively suppressed cccDNA accumation and more likely reduced cccDNA in liver tissues.
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot and qPCR data shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: 2H5-A14 can mediate immune effector cells to kill HBV-infected cells in vitro via ADCC and ADCP.
source: Our data showed that 2H5-A14 can mediate immune effector cells to kill HBV-infected cells in vitro via ADCC and ADCP, although more evdience is needed, it is conceivable to speculate that the clearance of cccDNA-carrying infected cells or decrease their in vivo half-lives by Fc-dependent effector functions via FcγR engagement, including cytotolytic and/or noncytolytic mechanisms, may have contributed to the anti-HBV effect of 2H5-A14 in a manner beyond Fab-mediated blockage of new infections.
evidence: This is supported by ADCC and ADCP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Six anti-preS1 human nAbs were identified from a phage library.
source: In summary, we identified six anti-preS1 human nAbs from a phage library and then improved the lead hit into 2H5-A14, a high-affinity and broad-spectrum nAb that is extremely potent in vitro and in vivo against both HDV and HBV.
evidence: This is supported by the antibody selection data presented in the Results section.

claim: 2H5-A14 is a high-affinity and broad-spectrum nAb that is extremely potent in vitro and in vivo against both HDV and HBV.
source: In summary, we identified six anti-preS1 human nAbs from a phage library and then improved the lead hit into 2H5-A14, a high-affinity and broad-spectrum nAb that is extremely potent in vitro and in vivo against both HDV and HBV.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization and animal efficacy data shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: 2H5-A14 inhibits NTCP binding by recognizing a structurally-defined and highly-conserved epitope located in close proximity to the RBS of preS1.
source: 2H5-A14 inhibits NTCP binding by recognizing a structurally-defined and highly-conserved epitope located in close proximity to the RBS of preS1.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data and competition assays shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: 2H5-A14 is capable of triggering epitope-specific and Fc-dependent effector functions.
source: 2H5-A14 is also capable of triggering epitope-specific and Fc-dependent effector functions.
evidence: This is supported by ADCC and ADCP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The effector functions contribute substantially to the anti-viral effect of 2H5-A14 against HBV infection in vivo.
source: Importantly, the effector functions contribute substantially to the anti-viral effect of 2H5-A14 against HBV infection in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of 2H5-A14 and 2H5-A14-DANA in the HBV treatment model shown in Figure 5.

claim: A nAb targeting the RBS adjacent region on preS1 can exert anti-HBV effect through Fc-dependent effector functions by engaging FcγRs.
source: These results for the first time demonstrate a nAb targeting the RBS adjacent region on preS1 can exert anti-HBV effect through Fc-dependent effector functions by engaging FcγRs, pointing toward a novel antibody-Fc-dependent strategy for HBV treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.
